exercises.title: Speaking: answer a WHY question with REASON × 3
exercises.instruction: 15 seconds to think, then record a 60–75 second answer. Start with a sentence signalling several reasons, cover all three levels (psychological / practical / social), develop each reason in one sentence, and finish with a conclusion.

items.prompt: Why do people take photographs of almost everything nowadays?
items.sampleAnswer: People photograph almost everything now for several interconnected reasons. Psychologically speaking, taking a picture gives a sense of holding onto a moment that would otherwise slip away — it's a very human response to the feeling that time passes too quickly. From a practical standpoint, the barrier has essentially disappeared: everyone carries a high-quality camera, storage is effectively unlimited, and it costs nothing, so there's no reason not to. And on a social level, photos have become a form of communication in themselves — a way of showing where you are and who you're with, rather than describing it. For all these reasons, I think the habit is less about photography in the traditional sense and more about documenting and sharing a life.
items.sampleNote: Khung REASON × 3: câu mở báo trước nhiều lý do, rồi đủ ba tầng tâm lý → thực tế → xã hội; không dùng "because".

items.prompt: Why do people enjoy watching sport rather than playing it?
items.sampleAnswer:
There are several interconnected reasons for this. Psychologically speaking, watching sport offers all the excitement and emotional highs without any of the risk — you get the drama of a last-minute goal without having to be fit enough to score it.

From a practical standpoint, playing a sport demands time, equipment and usually a group of people, whereas watching it requires nothing more than a phone or a TV, which suits busy adult lives far better.

On a social level, following a team creates a real sense of belonging. Supporters share a common identity, and big matches turn into a reason for friends and families to get together.

For all these reasons, I think watching sport has become less a substitute for playing and more a form of social connection in its own right.
items.sampleNote: Khung REASON × 3: tầng tâm lý (Psychologically speaking) → thực tế (From a practical standpoint) → xã hội (On a social level). Không có từ "because" nào; câu kết có sắc thái chứ không tóm tắt lại.

exercises.title: Speaking: a nuanced opinion answer
exercises.instruction: 15 seconds to think, then record a 60–80 second answer. The opening must be nuanced (NOT a bare Yes/No); give one supporting side with an example and one limitation, and finish by choosing a side with a condition.

items.prompt: Do you think people today are happier than people were fifty years ago?
items.sampleAnswer: To a certain extent, yes, but I'd stop short of saying it's a straightforward improvement. On one hand, people today have access to things that materially improve quality of life — better healthcare, more personal freedom, and far more choice in how they live. Someone with a chronic illness fifty years ago simply had fewer options. On the other hand, rates of anxiety and loneliness appear to have risen, partly because the same freedom that expands choice also removes the ready-made communities people used to belong to. On balance, I'd say people are better off in objective terms, but whether they feel happier depends heavily on whether they've managed to rebuild the sense of belonging that older, less mobile societies provided by default.
items.sampleNote: Khung NUANCED OPINION: To a certain extent… but I'd stop short of… → On one hand / On the other hand → On balance có điều kiện.

items.prompt: Do you think it is important for adults to keep learning new skills?
items.sampleAnswer:
To a large extent, yes — though I'd stop short of saying every adult needs to be constantly retraining.

On one hand, the job market is changing so quickly that skills which were valuable ten years ago can become obsolete almost overnight; someone who learns new software or data tools is far more likely to stay employable. Learning also has well-documented benefits for mental health, particularly in later life.

On the other hand, the pressure to keep "upskilling" can become exhausting, especially for people who are already working long hours or raising children, and not every skill needs to be career-related to be worthwhile.

On balance, I think lifelong learning is genuinely valuable, but only when it's driven by curiosity or real need rather than by anxiety about falling behind.

exercises.title: Speaking: answer an Advantages / Disadvantages question
exercises.instruction: 15 seconds to think, then record a 70–90 second answer. Give two benefits (at least one with an example), one REAL drawback with someone who loses out, use while or whereas, and finish with the trade-off condition.

items.prompt: What are the advantages and disadvantages of children using tablets at school?
items.sampleAnswer: Using tablets in class is very much a double-edged sword. The main benefit is access — a single device replaces a whole shelf of textbooks, and interactive material can adapt to a child's level in a way a printed page can't. There's also an equity argument: schools that lend devices can put resources in the hands of children whose families couldn't afford them. That said, it comes at a cost. A significant drawback is that constant screen access makes sustained attention harder, and the children hit hardest are those who already struggle to focus — for them the tablet becomes a source of distraction rather than learning. On balance, I'd say tablets are worth using, provided that schools are deliberate about when screens are on and when they're off, rather than treating the device as a default.
items.sampleNote: Khung BENEFIT – DRAWBACK – BALANCE: "double-edged sword", bất lợi nêu rõ ai chịu thiệt, kết luận có điều kiện.

items.prompt: What are the advantages and disadvantages of tourism for a small town?
items.sampleAnswer:
Tourism is very much a double-edged sword for a small town. The most obvious benefit is economic: visitors spend money in local cafés, guesthouses and shops, which creates jobs in places where young people might otherwise have to move to the city. It can also help preserve local traditions, since crafts and festivals suddenly have an audience willing to pay for them.

That said, the costs tend to fall on residents rather than on businesses. Rents and property prices rise, so long-term locals — especially older people on fixed incomes — can be priced out, and quiet streets become crowded and noisy.

On balance, I'd say tourism is beneficial provided the town manages its growth, for example by limiting new hotels and making sure part of the income goes back into local services.
items.sampleNote: Khung BENEFIT – DRAWBACK – BALANCE: hai lợi ích, bất lợi nêu rõ AI chịu thiệt (người dân lâu năm, người già thu nhập cố định), kết luận có điều kiện (provided…).

Câu 1 — What are the advantages and disadvantages of children using tablets at school?
Using tablets in class is very much a double-edged sword. The main benefit is access — a single device replaces a whole shelf of textbooks, and interactive material can adapt to a child's level in a way a printed page can't. There's also an equity argument: schools that lend devices can put resources in the hands of children whose families couldn't afford them. That said, it comes at a cost. A significant drawback is that constant screen access makes sustained attention harder, and the children hit hardest are those who already struggle to focus — for them the tablet becomes a source of distraction rather than learning. On balance, I'd say tablets are worth using, provided that schools are deliberate about when screens are on and when they're off, rather than treating the device as a default.

Câu 2 — What are the advantages and disadvantages of tourism for a small town?
Tourism is very much a double-edged sword for a small town. The most obvious benefit is economic: visitors spend money in local cafés, guesthouses and shops, which creates jobs in places where young people might otherwise have to move to the city. It can also help preserve local traditions, since crafts and festivals suddenly have an audience willing to pay for them.

That said, the costs tend to fall on residents rather than on businesses. Rents and property prices rise, so long-term locals — especially older people on fixed incomes — can be priced out, and quiet streets become crowded and noisy.

items.prompt: How is the way people communicate with friends today different from twenty years ago?
items.sampleAnswer: The way friends communicate has changed considerably over the past twenty years, mainly because of smartphones. In terms of frequency, contact used to be occasional — a phone call or a meet-up — whereas now it's almost continuous, a low-level stream of messages throughout the day. In terms of depth, though, the picture is more mixed: earlier conversations were fewer but longer and more focused, whereas a lot of messaging today is fragmented and easy to half-ignore. That said, the two still share common ground — when something serious happens, people still reach for a call, because they instinctively know text isn't enough. items.prompt: What can be done to reduce the level of stress people experience at work?
items.sampleAnswer: The root cause of workplace stress, I think, isn't individual time management but the way work is structured. In many organisations, staff are given more responsibility than the hours actually allow, and the culture treats long hours as a sign of commitment. A more effective approach might be for employers to redesign workloads around realistic capacity and to protect time off explicitly — but that has to come from senior management, not from individual employees, because a single person taking evenings off in a culture that rewards overwork simply falls behind. Of course, that alone wouldn't solve everything, because some stress comes from economic insecurity that no employer can fix. Ultimately it requires a combination of company policy, sensible regulation on working hours, and a broader cultural shift away from equating exhaustion with dedication.
items.sampleNote: Khung 5A: nêu nguyên nhân GỐC (cách tổ chức công việc) chứ không phải triệu chứng, giải pháp có chủ thể rõ ràng và có giới hạn.

items.prompt: Should the government be responsible for providing housing for low-income families?
items.sampleAnswer:
I think governments do have a central role here, but it's more about creating the conditions for affordable housing than simply handing out homes.

Only governments can make the large-scale decisions that actually shape the housing market — releasing land, setting planning rules and funding social housing that private developers have little incentive to build. Without that, low-income families are left competing in a market where prices rise far faster than wages.

That said, I would be cautious about the state trying to do everything itself. Large public housing estates have sometimes concentrated poverty in one area and been poorly maintained. A better approach might be partnerships, where developers must include a share of affordable flats in every new project.

So yes, the responsibility starts with the government, but it shouldn't end there.

items.prompt: Why do some students perform much better than others in the same class?
items.sampleAnswer: That's a 'why' question, so I'll give a few reasons at different levels. Psychologically, some students carry a heavier fear of failure — often tied to how their family talks about grades — and that anxiety actually interferes with performance rather than driving it. From a practical standpoint, out-of-school support is unevenly distributed: a child with quiet study space and access to private tuition has a structural advantage over one who doesn't, regardless of ability. And on a social level, classrooms tend to develop expectations — a student labelled early as 'weak' often internalises that and disengages. For all these reasons, I'd argue that gaps within a single class are less about raw talent and more about the conditions surrounding the child, which is why a genuinely student-centred approach tries to identify and remove those specific obstacles.

items.prompt: Should schools teach subjects like cooking and money management?

On balance, I think a short, practical course in the final years of secondary school would be worthwhile — not as another exam subject, but as genuine preparation for independent life.

items.prompt: Do you think people rely too much on their smartphones?
items.sampleAnswer: To a certain extent, yes, but I don't think it's as simple as over-reliance. In some respects the smartphone has clearly reduced effort: navigation apps mean we don't memorise routes, autocorrect compensates for weak spelling, and translation apps do a lot of work that used to require real study. There is a reasonable argument that this steady reduction in friction lowers our tolerance for difficulty. However, I would push back on calling that dependence, because the same device also frees up attention that routine tasks used to consume — whether people spend that freed-up time well is a question of discipline, not of the phone. On balance, I'd say the smartphone amplifies existing tendencies rather than creating new ones: a motivated person uses it to do more, and a distracted person uses it to avoid things. The tool is fairly neutral — the user isn't.
items.sampleNote: Trả lời hai chiều, nêu công nghệ cụ thể (navigation apps, …) thay vì "technology" chung chung, có câu tự phản bác.

items.prompt: Will people still need to learn foreign languages in the future?
items.sampleAnswer:
Looking at current trends, it's tempting to say no. Real-time translation apps and the live interpreting features on new smartphones are improving remarkably quickly, and for basic tasks — ordering food, reading a sign, writing a simple email — they're already good enough.

That said, I don't think they'll replace language learning altogether. Translation tools handle words, but they still struggle with humour, tone and cultural context, which is exactly what matters in a job interview, a negotiation or a friendship. There's also a cognitive argument: learning a language trains your memory and changes the way you think, which no device can do for you.

So my prediction is that fewer people will learn languages out of pure necessity, but those who do will stand out even more, precisely because genuine fluency will become rarer.

items.prompt: Why do some people not take environmental problems seriously?
items.sampleAnswer: There are a few reasons, and they operate at different levels. Psychologically, the threat feels abstract and distant — biodiversity loss and rising emissions don't produce an immediate, visible consequence for most people, so the brain deprioritises them. From a practical standpoint, acting sustainably often costs more or takes more effort, and for households already under financial pressure that trade-off isn't realistic. And on a systemic level, there's a fair amount of greenwashing, which leaves people cynical about whether anything they do matters. It's also worth noting that responsibility is often framed as purely individual, when a disproportionate share of emissions actually comes from a small number of large industrial actors. So I'd say the indifference is partly rational: people sense that individual action is necessary but not sufficient, and without visible stringent regulation, the incentive to bother is weak.

items.prompt: Should companies be legally responsible for the environmental damage they cause?
items.sampleAnswer:
Yes, I think they should, and it's largely a question of fairness. When a factory dumps waste into a river or a company's emissions damage air quality, the costs are paid by local communities — through health problems and lost livelihoods — rather than by the business that made the profit. Making companies legally responsible, in line with the "polluter pays" principle, forces them to include those costs in their decisions.

Voluntary pledges clearly aren't enough; many firms already engage in greenwashing, presenting themselves as eco-friendly while changing very little.

That said, the law needs to be realistic. If penalties are so strict that small businesses can't survive, production may simply move to countries with weaker regulation. So I'd support clear legal liability, combined with support for companies that genuinely invest in cleaner technology.

items.prompt: Why do fewer people know their neighbours than in the past?
items.sampleAnswer: There are a few structural reasons. Urbanisation means most people now live where the work is rather than where their family is, so the neighbourhood is a temporary base, not a community. Digital connectivity partly fills the gap, but online contact tends to be with people who are already friends, not with the person next door. And mobile lifestyles — the fact that people move every few years — means nobody has the incentive to invest in local relationships that they'll leave behind anyway. The result is measurable: higher loneliness and lower social trust. I'd also add that the capacity to engage is heavily shaped by economic circumstances — someone working long hours or two jobs simply doesn't have the evenings free that neighbourly contact tends to require, so this isn't really a question of people caring less.
items.sampleNote: Nêu CƠ CHẾ (đô thị hoá, giờ làm việc…) chứ không chỉ mô tả hiện tượng.

items.prompt: Should young people be required to do a period of community service?
items.sampleAnswer:
I can see the appeal, but I'd stop short of making it compulsory. On one hand, community service can do a lot of good: it brings young people into contact with groups they'd rarely meet otherwise, such as elderly people or families in poorer areas, and it can build a sense of responsibility that classroom lessons simply can't.

On the other hand, a mandatory scheme raises practical problems. Not every young person can afford to give up several months — some are already working to support their families, so the burden would fall unequally on those who can least afford it. There's also a risk that forced volunteering becomes a box-ticking exercise that nobody takes seriously.

On balance, I think governments should make community service attractive — for instance, by counting it towards university applications — rather than requiring it by law.

items.prompt: Why is work-related stress becoming more common in many countries?
items.sampleAnswer: It's tempting to say people just don't manage their time well, but the reasons are more structural. Time pressure is the main one: in economies where long hours are normalised and commuting eats up two hours a day, the space for recovery simply isn't there. There's also a cost dimension — proper time off, counselling, or even a quieter place to live all cost money, so the people most exposed to work-related stress are often least able to buy their way out of it. And the environment reinforces it: if a workplace culture treats being constantly available as a sign of commitment, then switching off carries a real career risk. If employers rewarded output rather than hours, a lot of this would ease. So I'd argue the solution is less about individual resilience and more about redesigning the environment in which people make these decisions.

items.prompt: What can governments do to improve public health?
items.sampleAnswer:
I think the most effective measures target the environment people live in, rather than relying on individual willpower.

Firstly, governments can make healthy choices cheaper and unhealthy ones more expensive — a tax on sugary drinks, for example, has reduced consumption in several countries. Thirdly, prevention is far cheaper than treatment, so free health check-ups and vaccination programmes save money in the long run.

That said, information campaigns alone rarely change behaviour — most people already know fast food is unhealthy. Many of the biggest health problems are linked to long working hours and low incomes, so real improvements need economic as well as medical policy.

items.prompt: Why do many young people prefer flexible work to a permanent job?
items.sampleAnswer: There are a few reasons operating at different levels. At the individual level, younger workers tend to prioritise autonomy — they want to decide when and where they work, which matters more to them than it did to their parents. Economically, the traditional bargain has weakened: a permanent job used to guarantee security and a rising income, but given that wages have stagnated and layoffs are common, flexibility now looks like a fairer trade — you give up stability you might not have had anyway, and gain control. And socially, having grown up watching the gig economy normalise, they simply don't see a permanent contract as the default marker of a successful career. That said, this preference is partly a rationalisation of insecurity — many would take a stable, well-paid permanent role if one were genuinely on offer.
items.sampleNote: Có ít nhất hai tầng động lực (cá nhân, kinh tế) và nhắc yếu tố kinh tế cụ thể.

items.prompt: Will people still work five days a week in fifty years?
items.sampleAnswer:
Looking at current trends, I think the five-day week is likely to become less universal, though I'd be cautious about predicting its disappearance.

Several companies, and even some countries, have already trialled a four-day week, and many reported that productivity stayed the same while staff were noticeably less stressed. Automation and AI will probably accelerate this, since routine tasks that take hours today may take minutes in the future.

That said, the change won't happen evenly. Jobs that depend on being physically present — nursing, construction, hospitality — are much harder to compress, and in lower-income economies many people may still need to work long hours simply to make ends meet.

So my prediction is that working patterns in fifty years will be far more varied: shorter weeks in some professions, but not a universal shift for everyone.
items.sampleNote: Dự đoán có lực đẩy cụ thể (thử nghiệm tuần 4 ngày, tự động hoá) và có caveat bắt buộc (the change won't happen evenly…).

items.prompt: What problems can too many tourists cause for a small town?
items.sampleAnswer: Too many tourists tend to cause problems that fall on residents rather than on the town as a whole. Economically, the benefits are real but unevenly distributed — a significant proportion is captured by property owners and large operators, while ordinary residents face the downsides. As short-term rentals spread, long-term residents are gradually priced out of the centre; peak-season crowds strain infrastructure that was built for a much smaller population; and the character that made the town attractive in the first place slowly erodes as shops shift to serving visitors rather than locals. There are social costs too: a sense that the place no longer belongs to the people who live there. So the core problem is not tourism itself but the fact that a small town has little capacity to absorb sudden, concentrated demand.

items.prompt: What advantages can tourism bring to a city?
items.sampleAnswer:
Tourism can bring substantial benefits to cities, though those benefits are distributed unevenly and come with real costs.

The most direct advantage is economic. Visitor spending generates revenue for hotels, restaurants, transport and retail, creating jobs across a wide spectrum of skill levels. In cities with significant historical assets, tourism can become a major economic pillar — think of how central it is to Venice, Kyoto or Prague.

Beyond economics, tourism plays a meaningful role in cultural preservation. Revenue generated by visitor interest often funds the conservation work that local governments could not otherwise afford. In that sense, tourism and heritage can form a virtuous cycle.

There are softer benefits too — the presence of international visitors exposes residents to different perspectives and ways of life, which enriches the cultural texture of a city over time.

That said, it would be dishonest to ignore the downsides. Over-tourism prices local residents out of their own neighbourhoods, strains infrastructure, and erodes the very authenticity that made a place attractive in the first place. The challenge for planners is harnessing the economic benefits while managing the social and environmental costs — a balance very few cities have achieved.

exercises.instruction: 15 seconds to think, then record an 80–95 second answer. Explain the MECHANISM (engagement-driven design), cover both the empowering and the harmful side, use precise terms (not "fake news" for everything), and include at least one advanced concession clause.

items.prompt: Why does false information spread so quickly online?
items.sampleAnswer: It spreads quickly because the structure of the platforms rewards it. These systems are designed to maximise engagement rather than well-being, so an algorithmically curated feed favours whatever provokes a strong reaction — and false or exaggerated claims tend to be more surprising, and therefore more shareable, than careful corrections. There's also a timing asymmetry: a dramatic claim reaches a large audience within hours, whereas a fact-check arrives days later to a fraction of the same people. Add algorithmic bias and echo chambers, and users mostly encounter information that already fits their existing beliefs, which lowers their guard. Whilst it's true that the same openness has given genuine visibility to marginalised voices and enabled real citizen journalism, the same mechanism that empowers those voices also accelerates misinformation — the design doesn't distinguish between the two.
items.sampleNote: Nêu được cơ chế thiết kế nền tảng (tối đa hoá tương tác) chứ không chỉ mô tả hiện tượng.

items.prompt: Should governments regulate what people can publish online?
items.sampleAnswer:
This is a difficult balance, so I'd argue for regulation, but of a limited kind.

On one hand, some content causes real harm — deliberate disinformation during elections or health crises, online harassment and scams — and platforms have shown they won't always remove it voluntarily, because outrage drives engagement. In those cases, clear laws requiring platforms to act quickly make sense.

On the other hand, giving governments broad power over what individuals can publish is risky. Vague rules about "false information" can easily be used to silence critics or journalists, which would undermine the very public debate that regulation is supposed to protect.

items.prompt: Why do some traditional art forms disappear while others survive?
items.sampleAnswer: It largely comes down to whether an art form can find a place in the modern economy. Traditional forms that can be adapted for performance, tourism or teaching tend to survive, because they generate revenue that funds their continuation. Forms that depended on a specific social ritual — a particular festival, a craft tied to a way of life that no longer exists — lose their function and fade, because the market simply doesn't price the social value they carried. Economically, younger people migrate to cities for work and the apprenticeship chains that transmitted these skills break. It's worth adding that this isn't uniform: in societies with strong state heritage protection or a deliberate cultural policy, forms survive that would disappear elsewhere. So the real question is not so much whether a tradition is 'valuable' as whether anyone has created the conditions — funding, teaching, visibility — in which it can still be practised.

items.prompt: Do you think globalisation is making cultures too similar?
items.sampleAnswer:
To some extent, yes, at least on the surface. You can now find the same coffee chains, fashion brands and streaming shows in almost every major city, and young people around the world often listen to the same music and use the same slang.

What worries me more is that traditional art forms which don't make money, such as certain styles of folk music, can quietly disappear, because the market underprices their social value.

exercises.instruction: Exam conditions: the examiner asks one question after another — do NOT stop. Record answers to all 5 questions, 60–90 seconds each. Identify the type and use the right framework for each one.

items.prompt: 1. Why do so many young people want to go to university?
items.sampleAnswer: There are several reasons, at different levels. Psychologically, university has become part of the expected life path — for many families, not going feels like falling behind. From a practical standpoint, a lot of well-paid careers still use a degree as a basic filter, so it functions as a gateway regardless of what you actually learn. And on a social level, it's also about the experience — moving away from home, building a network, and a few years of relative freedom before full-time work. So the degree itself is only part of the appeal.
items.sampleNote: Khung: REASON × 3.

items.prompt: 2. Do you think a university degree is still necessary to get a good job?
items.sampleAnswer: To a certain extent, but less than it used to be. On one hand, in fields like medicine, law or engineering it's still essential, and many employers use it to filter applications. On the other hand, in areas like tech, design or digital marketing, a strong portfolio and demonstrated skills increasingly matter more than the qualification. On balance, a degree still helps, but it's no longer the guarantee it once was — it's necessary in some fields and merely useful in others.
items.sampleNote: Khung: NUANCED OPINION.

items.prompt: 3. What are the advantages and disadvantages of studying while working?
items.sampleAnswer: It's very much a double-edged sword. The main benefit is that you apply what you learn immediately, so the knowledge sticks, and you graduate with real experience and no debt. That said, a significant drawback is the strain: something usually suffers — grades, work performance, or health — and the people hit hardest are those without a supportive employer who can offer flexible hours. On balance, it works well provided the workload is genuinely manageable and the employer is on board.
items.sampleNote: Khung: BENEFIT–DRAWBACK–BALANCE.

items.prompt: 4. How is the job market today different from your parents' generation?
items.sampleAnswer: It's changed considerably. In terms of security, my parents' generation could expect one employer, a clear promotion ladder and a pension, whereas now people change jobs every few years and job security is much weaker. In terms of skills, a qualification used to last a career, whereas today continuous retraining is more or less mandatory. That said, the two share common ground — both generations work hard and value being good at what they do. Ultimately, the biggest shift is that responsibility for a career has moved from the employer to the individual.
items.sampleNote: Khung: COMPARE.

items.prompt: 5. How do you think work will change in the next twenty years?
items.sampleAnswer: Looking at current trends, the clearest change will probably be driven by automation. Routine tasks are likely to be largely automated, which will shift human work towards judgement, creativity and managing the technology itself. We may also see the standard week become shorter or more flexible, given how much remote work has already normalised. That said, it's difficult to predict with any certainty, because these shifts depend heavily on regulation and on how businesses share the gains. A more cautious view is that change will be slower and more uneven than the headlines suggest.

items.prompt: 1. Why are some people not interested in environmental issues?
items.sampleAnswer: There are a few structural reasons. Psychologically, the threat feels abstract and distant — biodiversity loss and rising emissions don't produce an immediate, visible consequence, so the brain deprioritises them. From a practical standpoint, acting sustainably often costs more or takes more effort, and for households already under financial pressure that trade-off isn't realistic. And on a social level, a lot of greenwashing has left people cynical about whether anything they do matters. So the indifference is partly rational: people sense that individual action is necessary but not sufficient.
items.sampleNote: Khung: REASON × 3.

items.prompt: 2. Do you think individuals can make a real difference to the environment?
items.sampleAnswer: Individuals can make a meaningful difference, but it's worth being honest about the limits of individual action in isolation. On one hand, collective behaviour drives markets — when enough consumers refuse single-use plastics, producers adapt. On the other hand, a disproportionate share of global emissions comes from a small number of industrial actors, and framing the problem as purely personal can function as a deflection. On balance, individual action works best as part of a broader ecosystem of change that includes stringent regulation and corporate accountability.
items.sampleNote: Khung: NUANCED OPINION.

items.prompt: 3. What can local governments do to reduce waste in cities?
items.sampleAnswer: The root cause is that waste is currently cheaper to produce than to avoid, so the incentives are wrong. A more effective approach might be for city governments to make producers responsible for packaging through deposit-return schemes and to invest properly in separated collection and composting — households can only recycle what the system actually processes. Of course, that alone wouldn't solve everything, because many packaging decisions are made at national or corporate level. Ultimately it needs city policy, national regulation and consumer habits working together.
items.sampleNote: Khung: CAUSE–EFFECT–SOLUTION.

items.prompt: 4. How have attitudes towards the environment changed in your country?
items.sampleAnswer: They've shifted noticeably over the past couple of decades. It used to be a fringe concern discussed mainly by activists, whereas today it's fairly mainstream — recycling is normal, and younger people in particular factor it into everyday choices. This shift is largely driven by more visible extreme weather and by international pressure. That said, awareness hasn't fully translated into behaviour or policy, partly because economic growth is still the overriding priority. A more cautious view is that the change is real but shallow.
items.sampleNote: Khung: THEN–NOW–NEXT / COMPARE.

items.prompt: 5. Will cities be greener or more polluted in fifty years?
items.sampleAnswer: I think the most likely outcome is greener, but very unevenly. Wealthier cities are already retrofitting for heat and flooding, so we're likely to see a rapid expansion of green space, vertical planting and cleaner transport, driven mainly by climate pressure. Poorer, fast-growing cities may struggle to keep pace and could get worse before they improve. That said, it's difficult to predict with any certainty. On balance, I'd expect the average city to be cleaner than today, but the gap between rich and poor cities to widen.
items.sampleNote: Khung: TREND–PREDICTION–CAVEAT.

Wealthier cities are already retrofitting for heat and flooding, so we're likely to see a rapid expansion of green space, vertical planting and cleaner transport, driven mainly by climate pressure. Poorer, fast-growing cities may struggle to keep pace and could get worse before they improve. That said, it's difficult to predict with any certainty. On balance, I'd expect the average city to be cleaner than today, but the gap between rich and poor cities to widen.

exercises.instruction: The examiner asks one question after another — do not stop. Record answers to all 5 questions, 60–90 seconds each. Identify the type and use the right framework.

items.prompt: 1. Why do people spend so much time on social media?
items.sampleAnswer: For several interconnected reasons. Psychologically, these platforms are designed to maximise engagement, not well-being — an algorithmically curated feed delivers small, unpredictable rewards that are genuinely hard to put down. From a practical standpoint, a lot of social and even professional life now happens there, so stepping away has a real cost. And on a social level, there's a fear of missing out — if your friends are all coordinating and sharing on a platform, opting out means opting out of the group. So it's less pure choice than it looks.
items.sampleNote: Khung: REASON × 3.

items.prompt: 2. Do you think technology has brought people closer together?
items.sampleAnswer: To a certain extent, but it's more nuanced than a simple yes. On one hand, it has removed almost all the barriers to staying in touch — people maintain friendships across continents with minimal effort, and marginalised groups have found communities they could never have found offline. On the other hand, the same tools can make relationships shallower: a stream of low-effort messages isn't the same as sustained attention, and public broadcasting has replaced a lot of private conversation. On balance, technology has increased the quantity of connection while putting the quality under strain.
items.sampleNote: Khung: NUANCED OPINION.

items.prompt: 3. What are the benefits and drawbacks of working with artificial intelligence?
items.sampleAnswer: AI is very much a double-edged sword. The main benefit is that it frees up cognitive bandwidth — it handles routine drafting, summarising and analysis, letting people focus on judgement and creative work, and there's a productivity gain that can lower costs. That said, a significant drawback is deskilling: if junior staff never do the basic work themselves, they may not develop the judgement to check the AI's output, and they're the group hit hardest. On balance, the benefits outweigh the drawbacks provided organisations are deliberate about keeping humans genuinely in the loop.
items.sampleNote: Khung: BENEFIT–DRAWBACK–BALANCE.

items.prompt: 4. How is the way people make friends today different from in the past?
items.sampleAnswer: It's changed in a couple of significant ways. In terms of where friendships start, they used to form almost entirely through proximity — school, work, the neighbourhood — whereas now a large share begin online, around shared interests rather than shared location. In terms of maintenance, friendship used to require deliberate effort to stay in contact, whereas now a low level of contact happens passively through feeds and group chats. That said, they share common ground — people still value a small number of close, trusted friends above a large network. Ultimately, the biggest shift is that geography matters far less than it did.
items.sampleNote: Khung: COMPARE.

items.prompt: 5. How might communication change in the next generation?
items.sampleAnswer: Looking at current trends, communication is likely to become even more instant, visual and asynchronous — shorter messages, more voice notes and video, less real-time conversation. We may also see AI increasingly mediating messages — drafting, translating, summarising — which could smooth communication across languages but also make it harder to know what's genuinely a person's own voice. That said, it's difficult to predict with any certainty, and there are early signs of a counter-trend, with some people deliberately choosing slower, more personal forms of contact. On balance, I'd expect faster and more convenient communication, with a small but real backlash in favour of depth.
items.sampleNote: Khung: TREND–PREDICTION–CAVEAT.
